key_claims: Higher coffee consumption was associated with lower total and visceral fat and greater skeletal muscle mass, despite similar BMI.
Higher coffee intake was linked to lower circulating branched-chain amino acids, which are associated with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes risk.

In men, greater coffee consumption was associated with a more favorable glucose-insulin profile, higher total and bioavailable testosterone, and higher SHBG, but modestly lower free testosterone and free androgen index.
In women, higher coffee consumption was mainly associated with increased SHBG and lower free androgens.
The hormonal associations persisted after adjusting for BMI and lifestyle factors.
limitations: The study was observational and cannot establish causation.
The study was conducted in Finland, a country with high coffee consumption, which may limit generalizability.
The study only included participants aged 46 from the Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1966.
The findings require additional research before dietary recommendations can be made.
what_not_to_say: Coffee directly causes fat loss or muscle gain.
Coffee reduces the risk of type 2 diabetes or cardiovascular disease.
Coffee affects testosterone levels in all men or women.
The study proves that coffee is beneficial for health.
The study provides specific numbers or effect sizes for the associations.
